'''''Clarkia unguiculata''''' is a species of [[wildflower]] known by the common name '''elegant clarkia''' or '''mountain garland'''.<ref>{{PLANTS|id=CLUN|taxon=Clarkia unguiculata|access-date=29 November 2019}}</ref>

== Distribution and habitat ==
This plant is [[Endemism|endemic]] to [[California]], where it is found in many woodland [[habitat]]s.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Calscape |title=Elegant Clarkia |url=https://calscape.org/Clarkia-unguiculata-(Elegant-Clarkia) |access-date=2024-11-16 |website=calscape.org |language=en}}</ref> It grows along the coastal ranges of Mendocino and San Diego. ''Clarkia unguiculata'' can also be found in the Sierran foothills. Specifically, it is common on the [[forest floor]] of many [[oak woodland]]s, along with typical [[understory]] wildflowers that include ''[[Calochortus luteus]]'', ''[[Adelinia grandis]]'' and ''[[Delphinium variegatum]]''.<ref>C. Michael Hogan. 2009. [https://web.archive.org/web/20111004094242/http://www.globaltwitcher.com/artspec_information.asp?thingid=97686 ''Gold Nuggets: Calochortus luteus'', GlobalTwitcher.com, ed. N. Stromberg]</ref> It flowers in the summer and fall and thrives in somewhat neutral soil pH. Commonly found on open slopes or slightly shaded areas.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Clarkia unguiculata Elegant Fairyfan, Elegant clarkia PFAF Plant Database |url=https://pfaf.org/user/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Clarkia+unguiculata |access-date=2024-12-05 |website=pfaf.org}}</ref> These slopes are below {{convert|5000|ft}} and have dry conditions, where the plant thrives.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center - The University of Texas at Austin |url=https://www.wildflower.org/plants/result.php?id_plant=CLUN |access-date=2024-12-05 |website=www.wildflower.org}}</ref>

== Description ==
''C. unguiculata'' presents a spindly, hairless, waxy stem with a red hue. The species can grow up to {{cvt|3|ft|1}} tall with a small number of leaves populating the stem.<ref name="LBFWC-2004" /> The showy flowers have hairy, fused [[sepal]]s forming a cup beneath the corolla, and four petals each one to {{cvt|2.5|cm|1}} long.<ref>''Jepson Manual''. 1993. [http://ucjeps.berkeley.edu/cgi-bin/get_JM_treatment.pl?5263,5341,5404 ''Clarkia unguiculata'']</ref> The paddle-like petals come in shades of pink to reddish to purple and are slender and diamond-shaped or triangular in a [[raceme]] formation, in which each flower is connected to the main stalk by a pedicel, a short stem extension.<ref name="LBFWC-2004">{{Cite web |title=Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center - The University of Texas at Austin |url=https://www.wildflower.org/plants/result.php?id_plant=CLUN |access-date=2024-11-16 |website=www.wildflower.org}}</ref> There are eight long [[stamen]]s, the outer four of which have large red anthers. The [[Gynoecium|stigma]] protrudes from the flower and can be quite large. Its pistil is a long white structure, this combined with the red stamens allow this flower to be easily identifiable.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Clarkia unguiculata |url=https://ucjeps.berkeley.edu/eflora/eflora_display.php?tid=19605 |access-date=2024-12-05 |website=ucjeps.berkeley.edu}}</ref> The base of the stem has the leaves arranged in an opposite formation, however further up the stem the leaf arrangement becomes alternate. Produces a small indehiscent fruit, similar to a nut which hold the many little seeds.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Clarkia unguiculata |url=https://ucjeps.berkeley.edu/eflora/eflora_display.php?tid=19605#:~:text=Habit:%20Annual%20to%20perennial%20herb,flowers%201%20in%20axils;%20bracted. |access-date=2024-12-05 |website=ucjeps.berkeley.edu}}</ref>

== Ecology ==
[[File:Alypia mariposa 386216939.jpg|left|thumb|260x260px|[[Alypia mariposa|Mariposa forester]] larva on ''C. unguiculata'']]
''Clarkia unguiculata'' is pollinated by a variety of bees, butterflies and some bats.<ref name="LBFWC-2004" /> The main pollinator is ''[[Hesperapis regularis]]'', a native species of bees found in similar environments to ''C. unguiculata''.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Peach |first=Kristen |last2=Mazer |first2=Susan J. |date=April 2019 |title=Heteranthery in Clarkia : pollen performance of dimorphic anthers contradicts expectations |url=https://bsapubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/ajb2.1262 |journal=American Journal of Botany |language=en |volume=106 |issue=4 |pages=598–603 |doi=10.1002/ajb2.1262 |issn=0002-9122}}</ref> This plant has the ability to [[Self-pollination|self-pollinate]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Moeller |first=David A. |last2=Geber |first2=Monica A. |date=2005 |title=Ecological Context Of The Evolution Of Self-Pollination In Clarkia Xantiana: Population Size, Plant Communities, And Reproductive Assurance |url=http://www.bioone.org/perlserv/?request=get-abstract&doi=10.1554%2F04-656 |journal=Evolution |language=en |volume=59 |issue=4 |pages=786 |doi=10.1554/04-656 |issn=0014-3820|url-access=subscription }}</ref> This means the species is less reliant on the presence of pollinators like bees or butterflies to propagate itself.

The caterpillars of the [[Alypia mariposa|mariposa forester]] feed on it.<ref name="po">Powell, Jerry A. & Opler, Paul A. (2009).  ''Moths of Western North America''.  University of California Press, Berkeley and Los Angeles, CA. {{ISBN|978-0-520-25197-7}}</ref>

{{Clear|left}}

== Cultivation and uses ==
This species is cultivated in gardens, requiring dry air and dry soil for it to bloom.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center - The University of Texas at Austin |url=https://www.wildflower.org/plants/result.php?id_plant=CLUN |access-date=2024-12-09 |website=www.wildflower.org}}</ref>  It can be grown in any soil condition; sand, loamy or clay soils as long as the plant remains in dry conditions. As a [[hermaphrodite|hermaphroditic]] species, being pollinated by pollinators is very easy and requires less energy from the plant. The species cannot be grown in shaded areas, it must be exposed to the sun for majority of the day as it does not do well in cold conditions. If grown correctly, the seed will germinate within two weeks and bloom late summer and early fall.<ref>{{Cite web |title=medicinal herbs: ELEGANT FAIRYFAN - Clarkia unguiculata |url=https://www.naturalmedicinalherbs.net/herbs/c/clarkia-unguiculata=elegant-fairyfan.php |access-date=2024-12-09 |website=www.naturalmedicinalherbs.net}}</ref> 

Although not typically eaten, some parts of the plant are edible, specifically the seed. The seed can be eaten raw or cooked and ground into a fine powder.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Clarkia unguiculata Elegant Fairyfan, Elegant clarkia PFAF Plant Database |url=https://pfaf.org/user/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Clarkia+unguiculata |access-date=2024-12-09 |website=pfaf.org}}</ref>
